title: EnvironmentDefinition
description: How to create, start, deploy into, observe and reset one environment instance. The adapter implements the lifecycle (PLAN.md §5); this file only parameterises it.

adapter.description: A registered adapter kind (PLAN.md §5, §9). `local-web` is the MVP world; `local-db` is a file-backed one. Either way the adapter is an implementation of the lifecycle, not an environment: Veridian ships worlds, and a world may be simulated.

app.description: Directory of the application under test, relative to this file.

env.description: Environment variables. Values are treated as untrusted.

dependencyInstall.description: Command run once before start, inside `app`. Null means the app has no dependencies to install.

command.description: Executed verbatim, not through a shell string built from user input.

readyPattern.description: A regular expression matched against stdout to decide the app has started. Use this instead of sleeping.

url.description: Base URL of the running app, e.g. http://127.0.0.1:4317. Null or absent for a world reached by opening a file rather than over a socket - a database world has no address, and spelling that as an empty string would make 'this world has no address' indistinguishable from 'nobody filled the field in'.

api.description: The HTTP service this world is, when the world is one, and the smallest block in this document on purpose. Every other world block carries the facts that decide what its readings mean - a namespace, an account, a platform, an API version - because in those worlds a reading cannot supply them. A service is the one world where a reading supplies almost everything: the address comes from `url`, the readiness signal from `start.readyPattern`, the liveness answer from `health`. The one thing a reading cannot supply is its own subject - every request carries the address it was sent to and no statement of what was listening there - so this block holds exactly that and nothing else. It is separate from `url` rather than folded into it because `url` is an address and this is an identity: the same address serves whichever process happens to hold the port, so a bundle read later beside a result from another run would otherwise be unable to say whether the two judged the same service. A world declaring `api` is reached over a socket, exactly as a browser world is, so its `browser.enabled` defaults to true - a document for it states `browser: { enabled: false }`, because this world has an address but no page, and the browser policy follows the page rather than the address.

service.description: The service identity every reading names, so a result says which service produced it. A free string rather than an enumeration: a service name decides nothing a criterion can observe, and enumerating it would let a label act as a rule.

databasePath.description: Path of the database file this world is, relative to this file (or absolute). Present for a file-backed world such as `local-db`, where the application's state IS this file; absent for every other world. Stated here rather than as an adapter-private option so the plan every reader sees names the same file the adapter opens.

cluster.description: The cluster this world stands in for, when the world is a cluster. Present for a simulated cluster such as `sim-k8s`; absent for every other world. Same reasoning as `databasePath`: stated here rather than as an adapter-private option, so the plan every reader sees - the adapter, the bundle, a failure report - names the same cluster, namespace and registry the run measured, and so that 'this world is not a cluster' stays distinguishable from 'nobody filled the field in'.

name.description: The cluster name recorded in every reading, so a result says which cluster produced it.

namespace.description: The namespace this run is scoped to. A cluster is namespaced, and a criterion that named a bare object would be judged against whichever namespace happened to hold one.

images.description: Directory of built-image records, relative to `app`. The substitute registry holds exactly the images the application's own build produced, so a manifest naming a tag that was never built fails with an image-pull error for the real reason rather than for a knob someone set.

posix.description: The POSIX-like system this world stands in for, when the world is one. Present for a simulated system such as `sim-posix`; absent for every other world. Same reasoning as `cluster`: stated here rather than as an adapter-private option, so the plan every reader sees names the same distribution, account and sandbox root the run measured, and so that 'this world is not a system' stays distinguishable from 'nobody filled the field in'. A world declaring `posix` has no url and no cluster, exactly as a database world has no url.

distribution.description: The distribution the readings name, so a result says which system produced it.

user.description: The account the criteria act as. Readings are decided as this account, never as root - a hardening contract judged as root passes for a system no ordinary user can log into. The loader refuses `root` by name.

root.description: The sandbox directory, relative to `app`. The world's filesystem is rebuilt here on every reset, which is why it is a directory of the world's own rather than the application directory: resetting a world rooted at the application would delete the code under test.

os.description: The operating system this world stands in for, when the world is one. Present for a simulated system such as `sim-os`; absent for every other world. Same reasoning as `posix`: stated here rather than as an adapter-private option, so the plan every reader sees names the same family, release, account and sandbox root the run measured, and so that 'this world is not a machine' stays distinguishable from 'nobody filled the field in'. A world declaring `os` has no url, no cluster and no posix, exactly as a database world has no url.

family.description: Which system this world stands in for. It is the field that decides a path's spelling, the section separator, whether volumes fold case, and how the platform's configuration store is addressed - none of which the reading can supply on its own, because a reading that supplied them could not be contradicted by the plan that promised them.

system.description: The release the readings name, e.g. `Windows 11 23H2` or `macOS 14.5`. A record, not an installed image: the world has no ABI, and saying which release it stood in for is how a verdict stays traceable to a named substitute.

user.description: The account the criteria act as. Access is decided as this account, never as SYSTEM or root - a hardening contract judged as an account with every permission passes for a machine no ordinary account can log into. The loader refuses the privileged names by name.

root.description: The sandbox directory, relative to `app`. The world's filesystem is rebuilt here on every reset, which is why it is a directory of the world's own rather than the application directory: resetting a world rooted at the application would delete the code under test.

cloud.description: The cloud account this world stands in for, when the world is one. Present for a simulated account such as `sim-cloud`; absent for every other world. Same reasoning as `os`: stated here rather than as an adapter-private option, so the plan every reader sees names the same provider, region, account and principal the run measured, and so that 'this world is not an account' stays distinguishable from 'nobody filled the field in'. A world declaring `cloud` has no url, no cluster, no posix and no os, exactly as a database world has no url. There is deliberately no path here: a provider holds objects rather than directories, and every other simulated world carries a directory only because every other one has a filesystem.

provider.description: The provider identity the readings name, so a result says which account family produced it. A free string rather than an enumeration: a provider name decides nothing a criterion can observe, and enumerating it would let a label act as a rule.

region.description: The region the readings were taken in. A record, not a placement - the world has no data centre, and naming the region it stood in for is how a verdict stays traceable to a named substitute.

account.description: The account that holds every resource a reading reports. Distinct from `principal` on purpose: a decision is scoped to the account while being asked about the principal, and keeping both is what lets a workload's permissions be attached to the wrong identity.

principal.description: The identity the criteria act as. Access is decided as this principal, never as an account root - every policy in an account yields to its root, so a hardening contract judged as one is vacuously green. The loader refuses the privileged names by name, from the vocabulary that also decides what the substitute reports.

container.description: The container runtime this world stands in for, when the world is one. Present for a simulated runtime such as `sim-container`; absent for every other world. Same reasoning as `cloud`: stated here rather than as an adapter-private option, so the plan every reader sees names the same runtime, platform and sandbox the run measured, and so that 'this world is not a runtime' stays distinguishable from 'nobody filled the field in'. A world declaring `container` has no url, no cluster, no posix, no os and no cloud, exactly as a database world has no url. It is the first world block with two filesystems at once: `root` is a directory on this machine, while every path a container's command names is spelled inside the container by `platform` - and a bind mount names both in one command, which is why the declaration has to carry both a root and a platform rather than either alone.

runtime.description: The runtime identity the readings name, so a result says which runtime produced it. A free string rather than an enumeration: a runtime name decides nothing a criterion can observe, and enumerating it would let a label act as a rule.

platform.description: The platform the containers stand in for. It is a rule rather than a label - it decides how a path inside a container is spelled - so it is the one field in this block the loader validates, and a document naming a platform this substitution does not implement is refused before a world exists rather than judged with the wrong path grammar.

root.description: The directory on this machine the world's images, containers and volumes live in. A sandbox rather than the application directory, on the same reasoning as `posix.root`: the world is destroyed and rebuilt on every reset, so pointing it at the application would delete the code under test on the first iteration. It is also what lets the adapter tell a bind mount's host source from its in-container destination.

vscode.description: The VS Code extension host this world stands in for, when the world is one. Present for a simulated host such as `sim-vscode`; absent for every other world. Same reasoning as `container`: stated here rather than as an adapter-private option, so the plan every reader sees names the same host, API version and sandbox the run measured, and so that 'this world is not an extension host' stays distinguishable from 'nobody filled the field in'. A world declaring `vscode` has no url, no cluster, no posix, no os, no cloud and no container, exactly as a database world has no url. Two fields here earn their place in a way the earlier blocks' fields did not: `apiVersion` is what makes `engines.vscode` checkable at all - without it there is nothing for a manifest's declared floor to be compared against - and it is the one field that turns 'the extension loaded' into a verdict about whether it *should* have.

host.description: The host identity the readings name, so a result says which host produced it. A free string rather than an enumeration: a host name decides nothing a criterion can observe, and enumerating it would let a label act as a rule.

apiVersion.description: The VS Code API version this world answers as, e.g. `1.100.0`. A record, not an installation: there is no editor anywhere in the loop. It is the field that makes the engine floor computable - a real host refuses an extension whose `engines.vscode` range does not admit its own version, and this world computes the same answer from the same two facts, so an extension with a floor this host cannot meet is refused and a criterion can observe the refusal rather than wait for a user to report an extension that installs and never starts.

activationEvent.description: The activation event the host fires. Null - the default - means the manifest decides: the host fires the first event `contributes.activationEvents` or `activationEvents` declares, or `*` when it declares none. Declared explicitly only when a criterion is about *which* event activates the extension rather than about what activation does.

root.description: The directory on this machine the world's host, its persisted extension state and its workspace folder live in. A sandbox rather than the application directory, on the same reasoning as `posix.root`: the world is destroyed and rebuilt on every reset, so pointing it at the application would delete the code under test on the first iteration.

settings.description: Configuration values the operator supplies, as the workspace's own settings would. A setting an extension reads is either declared as a default by the manifest or supplied here, and the reading records which - so a criterion can tell 'the extension read the default' from 'the extension read the value it was told to read'. Without this field every setting would read as a default and the distinction would be unobservable, which is the shape of a field that exists and cannot be exercised.

process.description: The process boundary this world is, when the world is one. Present for `local-process`, which runs real child processes on this machine and reads the files they leave behind; absent for every other world. Same reasoning as `container` and `vscode`: stated here rather than as an adapter-private option, so the plan every reader sees names the same host, program and sandbox the run measured, and so that 'this world is not a process boundary' stays distinguishable from 'nobody filled the field in'. A world declaring `process` has no url, no cluster, no posix, no os, no cloud, no container and no vscode, exactly as a database world has no url. Unlike the six `sim-*` blocks, this one describes a world that is entirely real - a command here really runs and a file here really exists - so nothing in this block names a substitute, and its absence of a `simulated` field is a claim rather than an omission.

host.description: The host identity the readings name, so a result says which machine produced it. A free string rather than an enumeration: a host name decides nothing a criterion can observe, and enumerating it would let a label act as a rule.

application.description: The program this world starts and keeps running, or null when it starts none. Optional on purpose, and the optionality is the interesting part: every other world block names something the world *is*, while this one names something the world *may do*. A contract that provisions a tree with its own `run` steps and reads the files back has no use for a daemon, and requiring one would make the simplest shape of this world unwritable.

command.description: The program to run. Refused when empty: `application: null` is how a world says it starts no program, while an application without a command says it starts one and leaves the reader to guess which.

args.description: Its arguments, as a list rather than part of the command. A list is what lets a path containing a space be stated without quoting - the defect a shell-shaped spelling invites on Windows, where the same string reaches the program with different quoting rules depending on whether the runtime inserted a shell.

root.description: The directory on this machine the world's own files live in. A sandbox rather than the application directory, on the same reasoning as `posix.root`: this world creates and deletes files to observe what the application writes, and pointing it at the application would delete the code under test on the first iteration. It is required rather than defaulted because every path a criterion names is resolved inside it, so a defaulted root would judge a contract against whichever directory the process happened to be started in.

path.description: Appended to `url` to form the probe address. Null when there is no url to append to.

expectStatus.description: The status a healthy probe returns, defaulted only for a world reached over HTTP. Null hands the verdict to the adapter's own readiness signal, which is the only honest shape for a world that has no status to return.

reset.description: Reset is first-class (PLAN.md §20). A validator must never inherit contaminated state from a previous run.
